summary: The first astronauts on Mars will be 4 to 24 minutes from help by radio, on ground no one has walked. Existing Mars maps show regions; a crew needs the next 30 metres. WALKBACK plans one real Marswalk at the Mount Sharp boxwork ridges, where NASA's Curiosity rover drilled in 2025. It layers six kinds of NASA data on a 1 km site, computes the fastest safe walking route through five science stops, and checks it against NASA's published spacesuit limits. Its signature layer shows, for every point on the map, how many minutes the crew is from shelter. The plan is 1.80 km and 3 h 26 min long, never steeper than 19.3°, and never more than 34.1 minutes from the rover. On Mars the map has to carry the judgment that Mission Control carried on the Moon.
details:
We picked one spot on Mars and asked a simple question: if two astronauts walked out there, could a map keep them safe the whole way? The spot is the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, where the Curiosity rover spent most of 2025 drilling and taking photos. That gave us real ground truth to work with.

WALKBACK is a website that plans that walk. The crew parks a pressurized rover at the edge of the ridges, walks to five stops where Curiosity actually drilled, and walks back. The map shows the route, how steep every square meter is, and the thing we think matters most: how many minutes you are from the rover at any point. On Mars, help from Earth is 4 to 24 minutes away by radio, so the crew has to be able to answer that question on their own.

How we built it: we took the 1 meter elevation map of Gale Crater from USGS and NASA and worked out the slope everywhere. NASA says its new spacesuit can handle slopes up to 20 degrees, so anything steeper is off limits. We estimated walking speed with a hiking formula (Tobler's), scaled down to the 2 km/h pace NASA uses for planning moonwalks. That part is our assumption, and the app says so. Then a path-finding algorithm picks the fastest safe route between the stops, and running it backwards from the rover gives the minutes-to-shelter map.

What came out: a 1.8 km loop that takes about 3 hours 26 minutes, including 2 hours 20 minutes of science. The steepest step is 19.3 degrees, the crew is never more than 712 meters or 34 minutes from the rover, and all five safety checks pass. To test whether our slope map made sense, we laid Curiosity's real driving path over it: 93.5% of where the rover actually drove is ground our map calls walkable.

What's on the site: HiRISE and CTX images from orbit, THEMIS heat images, the slope map, Curiosity's real path, the radiation levels Curiosity measured there, daily weather Curiosity recorded on those exact days, and a card for each stop with a real rover photo and what the drill found (clay in a ridge, carbonate in a hollow). There's a solar storm drill based on the real storm Curiosity measured on May 20, 2024, which shows the fastest way back. There's also a helmet view that only shows six numbers, because an astronaut walking doesn't need a whole dashboard.

Why it matters: NASA plans moonwalks with a step-by-step process (pick science targets, check slopes, distance, time and supplies, then build the route). We tried to do the same thing for Mars, using data from the actual site instead of guesses. The same tool works anywhere there's an elevation map, so it could help plan routes for search and rescue or wildfire crews on Earth too. As far as we know, nobody has published a minutes-to-shelter map like this for a real Mars site, though route planners like MIT's SEXTANT came before us and inspired the approach.

Tools: Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Matplotlib, Pillow) in Google Colab for the data, and HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet for the website, hosted on GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/haarshaths-maker/walkback
